3. Core Concepts:

Shock Waves in Traffic Stream: A shock wave is the boundary between two different traffic states characterized by different densities and flows. It represents a discontinuity moving through the traffic stream.

Shock Wave Speed (\(u_w\)): The speed of the shock wave is geometrically represented by the slope of the chord connecting the two states on the \(q\)-\(D\) curve.\[u_w = \dfrac{q_B - q_A}{D_B - D_A} \]

Backward Forming Shock Wave: The most critical scenario occurs when a high-flow, uncongested traffic stream encounters a bottleneck.

  • State A (approaching): High flow, low density (e.g., Point 2).
  • State B (bottleneck queue): Lower flow, high density (e.g., Point 6).
  • Since arriving vehicles exceed the departure capacity (\(q_{\text{approach}} > q_{\text{bottleneck}}\)), a queue grows backward. The negative slope of the chord indicates the shock wave moves upstream.

  3. Option (D) — Point 4 to Point 5 (\(q_4 = q_5\)): Represents a stationary shock wave where flow is constant but density changes abruptly. The boundary between states does not move (\(u_w = 0\)). Not the typical shock wave scenario. ❌
  4. Option (B) — Point 2 to Point 6 (\(q_2 > q_6\)):

    • Vehicles arrive at rate \(q_2\) but are forced to a lower rate \(q_6\) at a restriction.
    • Since \(D_2 < D_6\), the slope is negative:\[u_w = \dfrac{q_6 - q_2}{D_6 - D_2} < 0 \]
    • This perfectly describes a backward forming shock wave — queue buildup at a bottleneck. This is the quintessential shock wave scenario in traffic design and operations. ✓

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Flow changing from point 2 to point 6, \(q_2 > q_6\) | Correct option: (B)

The flow-density relationship of traffic on a highway is shown in the figure



The correct representation of speed-density relationship of the traffic on this highway is
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Flow Fundamentals

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension / Analysis
  • Given Data: A triangular flow-density (\(q\)-\(k\)) curve starting at origin, rising linearly to peak flow (\(q_{max}\)) at optimal density (\(k_m\)), and then falling linearly to zero flow at jam density (\(k_j\)).
  • Aim: Identify the corresponding shape of the speed-density (\(v\)-\(k\)) relationship.

3. Core Concepts:

Fundamental Traffic Equation: Flow (\(q\)) is the product of density (\(k\)) and space-mean speed (\(v\)): \[q = k \cdot v \implies v = \dfrac{q}{k} \]

Piecewise Analysis: The given triangular \(q\)-\(k\) relationship has two distinct domains: Free-flow phase and Congested phase.

4. Solution Method & Execution:

Phase 1: Free Flow (\(0 \le k \le k_m\))
The \(q\)-\(k\) curve is a straight line passing through the origin.
Equation: \(q = C_1 \cdot k\) (where \(C_1\) is the slope, representing free-flow speed).
Finding speed: \(v = \dfrac{q}{k} = \dfrac{C_1 \cdot k}{k} = C_1\).
Result: Speed remains constant (a horizontal straight line) until density reaches \(k_m\).

Phase 2: Congested Flow (\(k_m \le k \le k_j\))
The \(q\)-\(k\) curve is a downward-sloping straight line terminating at \((k_j, 0)\).
Equation: \(q = C_2 \cdot (k_j - k)\) (where \(C_2\) is a positive constant).
Finding speed: \[v = \dfrac{q}{k} = C_2 \dfrac{k_j - k}{k} = C_2 \left(\dfrac{k_j}{k} - 1\right) \]
Result: This is the equation of a hyperbola. To determine its concavity:
\(v'(k) = -C_2 k_j / k^2 < 0\) (speed decreases as density increases).
\(v''(k) = 2C_2 k_j / k^3 > 0\) (the curve is strictly convex / concave-upward).

Conclusion: The correct graph must show a constant horizontal line initially, followed by a hyperbola that bows downwards (convex) towards the x-axis, tapering to \(v = 0\) at jam density.

6. Final Answer:

Correct option: The graph showing a flat horizontal line followed by a curve that is concave upwards (convex function) dropping to zero. (Option C)

questions.question: The design speed of a two-lane two-way road is 60 km/h and the longitudinal coefficient of friction is 0.36. The reaction time of a driver is 2.5 seconds. Consider acceleration due to gravity as 9.8 m/s². The intermediate sight distance (in m, round off to the nearest integer) required for the road is _________.
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Highway Geometric Design

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Road Type: Two-lane, two-way road
    • Design speed, \(V = 60\text{ km/h}\)
    • Longitudinal coefficient of friction, \(f = 0.36\)
    • Driver reaction time, \(t_r = 2.5\text{ s}\)
    • Acceleration due to gravity, \(g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2\)
  • Aim: Find the Intermediate Sight Distance (ISD) in meters, rounded to the nearest integer.

3. Core Concepts:

Stopping Sight Distance (SSD): The minimum sight distance required to stop safely. \[\text{SSD} = v \cdot t_r + \dfrac{v^2}{2gf} \] (where \(v\) must be in m/s)

Intermediate Sight Distance (ISD): As per IRC guidelines, when Overtaking Sight Distance (OSD) cannot be provided, ISD is used to allow overtaking with caution: \[\text{ISD} = 2 \times \text{SSD} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Convert design speed from km/h to m/s.
  2. Calculate SSD using the kinematic formula.
  3. Double the SSD to find ISD.
  4. Round to the nearest integer.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Unit Conversion

\[v = 60 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = 16.6667\text{ m/s} \]

Step 2: Calculate SSD

  • Lag distance \(= v \cdot t_r = 16.6667 \times 2.5 = 41.6667\text{ m}\)
  • Braking distance \(= \dfrac{v^2}{2gf} = \dfrac{(16.6667)^2}{2 \times 9.8 \times 0.36} = \dfrac{277.778}{7.056} = 39.3676\text{ m}\)
\[\text{SSD} = 41.6667 + 39.3676 = 81.0343\text{ m} \]

Step 3: Calculate ISD

\[\text{ISD} = 2 \times 81.0343 = 162.0686\text{ m} \]

Step 4: Rounding
Rounded to the nearest integer: \(\text{ISD} = 162\text{ m}\).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 162 m | Accepted key range: 154 to 178

    • Initial grade \(= +G\%\)
    • Final grade \(= +2G\%\) (doubled)

3. Core Concepts:

  • Braking Distance (\(L\)): On a gradient \(n\), the effective deceleration is modified by gravity along the slope:\[L = \dfrac{v^2}{2g_{acc}(f_r \pm n)} \]where \(n = G/100 = 0.01G\) in decimal format.
  • Percentage Change: \(\dfrac{L_{final} - L_{initial}}{L_{initial}} \times 100\)

4. Solution Method:

Formulate braking distances for both grades, find their algebraic difference, divide by the initial braking distance, and express as a percentage magnitude.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Initial braking distance (\(L_1\)):\[L_1 = \dfrac{v^2}{2g_{acc}(f_r + 0.01G)} \]
  2. Final braking distance (\(L_2\)) with doubled grade:\[L_2 = \dfrac{v^2}{2g_{acc}(f_r + 0.02G)} \]
  3. Change in braking distance (\(\Delta L = L_2 - L_1\)):\[ \Delta L = \dfrac{v^2}{2g_{acc}} \left[\dfrac{(f_r + 0.01G) - (f_r + 0.02G)}{(f_r + 0.02G)(f_r + 0.01G)} \right] = \dfrac{v^2}{2g_{acc}} \cdot \dfrac{-0.01G}{(f_r + 0.02G)(f_r + 0.01G)} \]
  4. Percentage change:\[\%\text{ Change} = \dfrac{\Delta L}{L_1} \times 100 = \dfrac{-0.01G}{(f_r + 0.02G)(f_r + 0.01G)} \times (f_r + 0.01G) \times 100 = \dfrac{-0.01G}{f_r + 0.02G} \times 100 \]

The absolute magnitude of the percentage decrease is:

\[\dfrac{0.01G}{f_r + 0.02G} \times 100 \]

6. Final Answer:

\(\%\text{ Change} = \dfrac{0.01G}{f_r + 0.02G} \times 100\) | Correct option: (A)

questions.question: The maximum number of vehicles observed in any five minute period during the peak hour is 160. If the total flow in the peak hour is 1000 vehicles, the five minute peak hour factor (round off to 2 decimal places) is ________
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Engineering

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Maximum vehicle volume in any 5-minute period, \(V_{5(\max)} = 160\) vehicles
    • Total overall volume in peak hour, \(V = 1000\) vehicles
    • Sub-interval duration, \(n = 5\) minutes
  • Aim: Calculate the 5-minute Peak Hour Factor (\(\text{PHF}_5\)), rounded to 2 decimal places.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Peak Hour Factor (PHF): Quantifies traffic volume fluctuation within the peak hour.\[\text{PHF}_n = \dfrac{\text{Total Hourly Volume}}{N \times \text{Maximum }n\text{-minute Volume}} \]where \(N = 60/n\) is the number of \(n\)-minute sub-intervals per hour.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Determine the number of 5-minute intervals in one hour (\(N\)).
  2. Compute the theoretical maximum hourly flow rate.
  3. Divide actual total volume by this theoretical maximum.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Number of intervals: \(N = 60/5 = 12\)
  2. Theoretical maximum hourly flow: \(12 \times 160 = 1920\) veh/hr
  3. \(\text{PHF}_5 = \dfrac{1000}{1920} = 0.52083 \approx 0.52\)

6. Final Answer:

\(\text{PHF}_5 = 0.52\) | Accepted key range: 0.51 to 0.53

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q45
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: Average free flow speed and the jam density observed on a road stretch are 60 km/h and 120 vehicles/km, respectively. For a linear speed-density relationship, the maximum flow on the road stretch (in vehicles/h) is ________
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Flow Theory

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Free flow speed, \(v_f = 60\) km/h
    • Jam density, \(k_j = 120\) veh/km
    • Linear speed-density relationship
  • Aim: Determine the maximum flow \(q_{\max}\) on the road stretch.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Greenshields Macroscopic Model: Assumes a linear relationship between speed (\(v\)) and density (\(k\)):\[v = v_f \left(1 - \dfrac{k}{k_j}\right) \]
  • Fundamental Traffic Equation: \(q = k \times v\)
  • Maximum Flow (\(q_{\max}\)): The parabolic \(q\)-\(k\) curve peaks at exactly half the jam density and half the free flow speed:\[q_{\max} = \dfrac{v_f \times k_j}{4} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Verify the model matches Greenshields (linear \(v\)-\(k\)).
  2. Directly apply the peak capacity formula.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

\[q_{\max} = \dfrac{60\text{ km/h} \times 120\text{ veh/km}}{4} = \dfrac{7200}{4} = 1800\text{ veh/h} \]

6. Final Answer:

\(q_{\max} = 1800\) veh/h | Accepted key range: 1800 to 1800

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q46
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: Traffic on a highway is moving at a rate of 360 vehicles per hour at a location. If the number of vehicles arriving on this highway follows Poisson distribution, the probability (round off to 2 decimal places) that the headway between successive vehicles lies between 6 and 10 seconds is ________
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Flow Theory

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Traffic volume/rate, \(\lambda = 360\) veh/h
    • Arrival distribution: Poisson
    • Headway bounds: \(t_1 = 6\) s and \(t_2 = 10\) s
  • Aim: Calculate the probability that the headway lies between 6 and 10 seconds.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Poisson Arrivals & Exponential Headways: If vehicle arrivals follow a discrete Poisson process, the time gaps (headways, \(h\)) between successive vehicles follow a continuous Exponential Distribution.
  • PDF: \(f(t) = \lambda e^{-\lambda t}\)
  • CDF: \(P(h < t) = 1 - e^{-\lambda t}\)
  • Probability between bounds: \(P(t_1 \le h \le t_2) = e^{-\lambda t_1} - e^{-\lambda t_2}\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Convert the flow rate (\(\lambda\)) into consistent units (vehicles per second).
  2. Apply the exponential distribution formula for the given bounds.
  3. Round to 2 decimal places.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Convert Flow Rate to per second:\[\lambda = \dfrac{360\text{ veh/h}}{3600\text{ s/h}} = 0.1\text{ veh/s} \]
  2. Calculate Probability:\[P(6 \le h \le 10) = e^{-\lambda \times 6} - e^{-\lambda \times 10} = e^{-0.6} - e^{-1.0} \]
  3. Evaluate:\[e^{-0.6} \approx 0.5488, \quad e^{-1.0} \approx 0.3679 \]\[P = 0.5488 - 0.3679 = 0.1809 \approx 0.18 \]

6. Final Answer:

\(P(6 \le h \le 10) = 0.18\) | Accepted key range: 0.17 to 0.19

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q47
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: A parabolic vertical curve is being designed to join a road of grade +5% with a road of grade –3%. The length of the vertical curve is 400 m measured along the horizontal. The vertical point of curvature (VPC) is located on the road of grade +5%. The difference in height between VPC and vertical point of intersection (VPI) (in m, round off to the nearest integer) is ________
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Geometric Design

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Initial Grade, \(n_1 = +5\% = +0.05\)
    • Final Grade, \(n_2 = -3\% = -0.03\)
    • Length of vertical curve, \(L = 400\) m
  • Aim: Find the difference in height between the Vertical Point of Curvature (VPC) and the Vertical Point of Intersection (VPI).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Parabolic Vertical Curves: By standard highway design geometry, a parabolic curve is tangent to the initial grade at the VPC and tangent to the final grade at the VPT.
  • Location of VPI: The intersection of the two tangents (VPI) is located exactly halfway along the horizontal length of the curve.
    Horizontal distance from VPC to VPI \(= \dfrac{L}{2}\).
  • The elevation changes simply by following the straight tangent line (gradient \(n_1\)) for a distance of \(\dfrac{L}{2}\).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Identify the horizontal distance to the VPI.
  2. Multiply this horizontal distance by the initial gradient slope (\(n_1\)) to find the height difference.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Determine Horizontal Distance:\[X = \dfrac{L}{2} = \dfrac{400}{2} = 200\text{ m} \]
  2. Calculate Elevation Difference:\[\Delta H = n_1 \times X = 0.05 \times 200\text{ m} = 10\text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

\(\Delta H = 10\) m | Accepted key range: 10 to 10

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q48
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: Tie bars of 12 mm diameter are to be provided in a concrete pavement slab. The working tensile stress of the tie bars is 230 MPa, the average bond strength between a tie bar and concrete is 2 MPa, and the joint gap between the slabs is 10 mm. Ignoring the loss of bond and the tolerance factor, the design length of the tie bars (in mm, round off to the nearest integer) is ________
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Highway Pavements

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Tie bar diameter, \(d = 12\) mm
    • Working tensile stress, \(f_t = 230\) MPa (N/mm\(^2\))
    • Average bond strength, \(\tau_{bd} = 2\) MPa (N/mm\(^2\))
    • Joint gap \(= 10\) mm
  • Aim: Find the design length of the tie bars as per standard codes.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Tie Bars in Rigid Pavement (IRC:58): Tie bars keep the longitudinal joints tightly closed. They are not load transfer devices like dowel bars.
  • The length of the tie bar must be sufficient to develop the full tensile strength of the bar via bond strength with the concrete.
  • Development Length (\(L_d\)): The length needed on one side of the joint, derived by equating pull-out force to bond resistance:\[\dfrac{\pi}{4} d^2 f_t = \pi d L_d \tau_{bd} \implies L_d = \dfrac{d \cdot f_t}{4 \cdot \tau_{bd}} \]
  • Total Design Length (\(L\)): The bar must be embedded by \(L_d\) on both sides of the joint gap:\[L = 2L_d + \text{Joint Gap} = \dfrac{d \cdot f_t}{2 \cdot \tau_{bd}} + \text{Joint Gap} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate the required development length \(L_d\) for one side.
  2. Multiply by 2 and add the joint gap.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Development Length (\(L_d\)):\[L_d = \dfrac{12 \times 230}{4 \times 2} = \dfrac{2760}{8} = 345\text{ mm} \]
  2. Calculate Total Tie Bar Length (\(L\)):\[L = 2(345) + 10 = 690 + 10 = 700\text{ mm} \]

6. Final Answer:

Tie Bar Length \(= 700\) mm | Accepted key range: 700 to 700

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q11
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: Structural failures considered in the mechanistic method of bituminous pavement design are
questions.explanation:
Highway Engineering | Pavement Design

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall
  • Given Data: Conceptual query regarding the mechanistic-empirical method for bituminous pavement design.
  • Aim: Identify the primary structural failure modes considered in this design philosophy.

3. Core Concepts:

Mechanistic-Empirical Design (IRC:37): This method calculates pavement responses (stresses and strains) using mechanistic models (like multi-layer elastic theory) and relates them to pavement performance using empirical distress models.

Critical Locations and Distresses:

  1. Fatigue Cracking: Caused by repeated horizontal tensile strains (\(\epsilon_t\)) at the bottom of the bituminous layer.
  2. Rutting: Caused by permanent deformation from repeated vertical compressive strains (\(\epsilon_z\)) at the top of the subgrade.

4. Solution Method:

According to Indian Roads Congress code IRC:37 (Guidelines for the Design of Flexible Pavements), the two primary structural failure criteria used to determine the thickness and layers of flexible (bituminous) pavements are Fatigue (bottom-up cracking) and Rutting (subgrade permanent deformation). Shear and Slippage are typically mitigated through material mix design (like Marshall stability) and tack coats, rather than governing the macro-structural thickness.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Recall the failure criteria as per IRC:37 multi-layer elastic design.
  2. Identify Fatigue (tensile strain parameter) and Rutting (compressive strain parameter).
  3. Match with the given options.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Fatigue and Rutting | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q19
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: The speed-density relationship in a mid-block section of a highway follows the Greenshield’s model. If the free flow speed is \(v_f\) and the jam density is \(k_j\), the maximum flow observed on this section is
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Engineering

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Greenshield's macroscopic speed-density model is applicable.
    • Free flow speed \(= v_f\)
    • Jam density \(= k_j\)
  • Aim: Find the expression for maximum flow (\(q_{max}\)) observed on this section.

3. Core Concepts:

Greenshield's Model: Assumes a linear relationship between space-mean speed (\(v\)) and density (\(k\)):

\[v = v_f \left(1 - \dfrac{k}{k_j}\right) \]

Fundamental Traffic Equation: Flow (\(q\)) is the product of speed and density: \(q = k \cdot v\).

4. Solution Method:

Substitute the velocity expression from Greenshield's equation into the fundamental traffic flow equation. This creates a parabolic (quadratic) relationship between flow and density. Differentiate the flow equation with respect to density and equate to zero to find the critical density that yields the maximum flow, then calculate the maximum flow.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Form Flow Equation:\[q = k \cdot v_f \left(1 - \dfrac{k}{k_j}\right) = v_f \cdot k - \dfrac{v_f}{k_j} \cdot k^2 \]
  2. Maximize Flow: Take the derivative \(\dfrac{dq}{dk}\) and set to zero.\[\dfrac{dq}{dk} = v_f - \dfrac{2v_f}{k_j} \cdot k = 0 \]
  3. Find Critical Density (\(k_c\)):\[v_f = \dfrac{2v_f \cdot k}{k_j} \implies k_c = \dfrac{k_j}{2} \]
  4. Find Critical Speed (\(v_c\)): Substitute \(k = \dfrac{k_j}{2}\) into the speed model.\[v_c = v_f \left(1 - \dfrac{k_j/2}{k_j}\right) = v_f \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{v_f}{2} \]
  5. Calculate Maximum Flow (\(q_{max}\)):\[q_{max} = k_c \cdot v_c = \left(\dfrac{k_j}{2}\right) \cdot \left(\dfrac{v_f}{2}\right) = \dfrac{v_f k_j}{4} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\dfrac{v_f k_j}{4}\) | Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q23
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: A vehicle is moving on a road of grade +4% at a speed of 20 m/s. Consider the coefficient of rolling friction as 0.46 and acceleration due to gravity as 10 m/s². On applying brakes to reach a speed of 10 m/s, the required braking distance (in m, round off to nearest integer) along the horizontal, is ______
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Stopping Sight Distance

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Initial speed, \(u = 20\) m/s
    • Final speed, \(v = 10\) m/s
    • Road grade, \(n = +4\%\)
    • Coefficient of longitudinal/rolling friction, \(f = 0.46\)
    • Gravity, \(g = 10\) m/s²
  • Aim: Compute the required braking distance along the horizontal.

3. Core Concepts:

Work-Energy Theorem: Loss of kinetic energy equals the work done by friction and gravity.

Formulas: For a sloping road:

\[s_{\text{slope}} = \dfrac{u^2 - v^2}{2g(f \cdot \cos\theta + \sin\theta)} \]

The horizontal distance is \(s_{\text{horizontal}} = s_{\text{slope}} \cdot \cos\theta\), which simplifies to:

\[s_{\text{horizontal}} = \dfrac{u^2 - v^2}{2g(f + \tan\theta)} \]

(This derivation proves why we directly add the gradient percentage to the friction factor to get horizontal distance!)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Establish the effective deceleration coefficient incorporating both tire friction and road gradient (+0.04 for an upward slope, acting as additional deceleration).
  2. Substitute the initial/final velocities into the rigorous horizontal stopping distance formula.
  3. Solve and round off to the nearest integer.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Effective Friction Factor:\[f_{eff} = f + \tan\theta = 0.46 + 0.04 = 0.50 \]
  2. Apply Work-Energy Formula (Kinematics):\[s_{\text{horizontal}} = \dfrac{u^2 - v^2}{2 \cdot g \cdot f_{eff}} = \dfrac{20^2 - 10^2}{2 \times 10 \times 0.50} \]
  3. Calculations:\[s_{\text{horizontal}} = \dfrac{400 - 100}{10} = \dfrac{300}{10} = 30 \text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 30 | Accepted key range: 30 to 30

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q34
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question:
A flexible pavement has the following class of loads during a particular hour of the day.
i. 80 buses with 2-axles (each axle load of 40 kN);
ii. 160 trucks with 2-axles (front and rear axle loads of 40 kN and 80 kN, respectively)

The equivalent standard axle load repetitions for this vehicle combination as per IRC:37-2012 would be
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Pavement Design

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Vehicle Class 1: 80 buses, 2 axles/bus, each axle = 40 kN
    • Vehicle Class 2: 160 trucks, 2 axles/truck, front = 40 kN, rear = 80 kN
  • Aim: Compute the equivalent standard axle load (ESAL) repetitions as per IRC:37-2012.

3. Core Concepts:

Equivalent Axle Load Factor (EALF) / Vehicle Damage Factor (VDF): Used to convert mixed traffic into equivalent repetitions of a standard axle.

Fourth Power Rule (IRC:37-2012):

\[EALF = \left( \dfrac{P}{P_s} \right)^4 \]

Where \(P\) = Actual Axle Load, \(P_s\) = Standard Axle Load (\(80\) kN for a single axle with dual wheels).

4. Solution Method & Execution:

  1. Step 1: Calculate VDF for one Bus
    A bus has 2 axles of 40 kN each.\[VDF_{\text{bus}} = 2 \times \left(\dfrac{40}{80}\right)^4 = 2 \times (0.5)^4 = 2 \times 0.0625 = 0.125 \]
  2. Step 2: Calculate VDF for one Truck
    A truck has one front axle of 40 kN and one rear axle of 80 kN.\[VDF_{\text{truck}} = \left(\dfrac{40}{80}\right)^4 + \left(\dfrac{80}{80}\right)^4 = (0.5)^4 + (1)^4 = 0.0625 + 1 = 1.0625 \]
  3. Step 3: Calculate Total ESAL Repetitions
    • ESAL from buses \(= 80 \times 0.125 = 10\) standard axles
    • ESAL from trucks \(= 160 \times 1.0625 = 170\) standard axles
    \[\text{Total ESAL} = 10 + 170 = 180 \text{ standard axles} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 180 | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q44
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: The uniform arrival and uniform service rates observed on an approach road to a signalized intersection are 20 and 50 vehicles/minute, respectively. For this signal, the red time is 30 s, the effective green time is 30 s, and the cycle length is 60 s. Assuming that initially there are no vehicles in the queue, the average delay per vehicle using the approach road during a cycle length (in s, round off to 2 decimal places) is ______
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Signals (Queuing Theory)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis / Application
  • Given Data:
    • Arrival rate (\(q\)): 20 veh/min
    • Service rate (\(s\)): 50 veh/min
    • Red time (\(r\)): 30 s
    • Effective green time (\(g\)): 30 s
    • Cycle length (\(C\)): 60 s
    • Initial queue: 0 vehicles
  • Aim: Calculate the average delay per vehicle (in seconds) during one cycle length.

3. Core Concepts:

Deterministic Queuing at Signals: Since arrival and service rates are uniform, random delay components are zero. The delay is entirely "uniform delay", found by evaluating the area of the queue accumulation polygon (a triangle).

Variables in standard units (veh/sec):

  • \(q = \dfrac{20}{60} = \dfrac{1}{3}\) veh/s
  • \(s = \dfrac{50}{60} = \dfrac{5}{6}\) veh/s

Total Delay (\(D\)): Area of the queue triangle \(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times (\text{Time queue exists}) \times (\text{Maximum queue})\)

Webster's Uniform Delay Formula (Alternative):

\[d_1 = \dfrac{C(1 - \lambda)^2}{2(1 - \lambda x)} \]

where \(\lambda = g/C\) and \(x = q/(\lambda s)\) (Degree of saturation).

4. Solution Method (Queue Polygon Method):

  1. Convert rates from veh/min to veh/s.
  2. Find the maximum queue length built up during the red phase.
  3. Calculate the time required to clear this queue during the green phase.
  4. Find the total delay (area of the queue-time triangle).
  5. Divide total delay by the total number of vehicles arriving in the cycle.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Conversion of units
    \(q = 20/60 = 0.333\) veh/s, \(s = 50/60 = 0.833\) veh/s
  2. Step 2: Queue buildup during Red time (\(r = 30\) s)\[Q_{\text{max}} = q \times r = \dfrac{1}{3} \times 30 = 10\text{ vehicles} \]
  3. Step 3: Queue dissipation during Green time
    Net discharge rate \(= s - q\). Time to clear queue:\[t_c = \dfrac{Q_{\text{max}}}{s - q} = \dfrac{10}{\dfrac{5}{6} - \dfrac{1}{3}} = \dfrac{10}{0.5} = 20\text{ s} \]Sanity Check: \(t_c\) (20 s) < Effective green time (30 s). Queue clears before green ends.
  4. Step 4: Total uniform delay (\(D\))
    Total time queue exists \(= r + t_c = 30 + 20 = 50\) s\[D = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 50\text{ s} \times 10\text{ veh} = 250\text{ veh-s} \]
  5. Step 5: Average delay per vehicle
    Total vehicles in one cycle \(= q \times C = \dfrac{1}{3} \times 60 = 20\) vehicles\[\text{Average delay} = \dfrac{250\text{ veh-s}}{20\text{ veh}} = 12.5\text{ s/veh} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 12.50 s/veh | Accepted key range: 12.00 to 13.00

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q45
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: A broad gauge railway line passes through a horizontal curved section (radius = 875 m) of length 200 m. The allowable speed on this portion is 100 km/h. For calculating the cant, consider the gauge as centre-to-centre distance between the rail heads, equal to 1750 mm. The maximum permissible cant (in mm, round off to 1 decimal place) with respect to the centre-to-centre distance between the rail heads is ______
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Railway Geometric Design

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Radius of curve (\(R\)): 875 m
    • Length of curve (\(L\)): 200 m (Distractor data)
    • Allowable speed (\(V\)): 100 km/h
    • Gauge (\(G\)): 1750 mm = 1.750 m (Centre-to-centre distance between rail heads)
  • Aim: Determine the maximum permissible (equilibrium) cant in mm, rounded to 1 decimal place.

3. Core Concepts:

Superelevation (Cant): The elevation of the outer rail above the inner rail at a horizontal curve to counteract centrifugal force.

Equilibrium Cant Formula: Derived from basic mechanics where centrifugal force is balanced by the gravity component of the canted track.

\[e = \dfrac{G \cdot v^2}{g \cdot R} \]

Where \(v\) is speed in m/s, \(g = 9.81\) m/s².

Standard Engineering Practical Formula: By substituting \(v = V/3.6\):

\[e = \dfrac{G \cdot V^2}{127 \cdot R} \]

(Using exactly \(g = 9.81\) gives a denominator constant of 127.14, but 127 is the standard code-adopted constant in India.)

4. Solution Method:

Apply the exact equilibrium cant formula, keeping \(G\) in mm to obtain \(e\) directly in mm.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Method 1: Exact Fundamental Calculation (\(g = 9.81\) m/s²)

  1. Convert speed to m/s: \(v = 100 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = 27.778\) m/s
  2. Substitute into equilibrium equation:\[e = \dfrac{1750\text{ mm} \times (27.778)^2}{9.81 \times 875} = \dfrac{1750 \times 771.605}{8583.75} = 157.31\text{ mm} \]

Method 2: Using standard codal constant (127)

\[e = \dfrac{G \cdot V^2}{127 \cdot R} = \dfrac{1750 \times (100)^2}{127 \times 875} = \dfrac{17{,}500{,}000}{111{,}125} = 157.48\text{ mm} \]

Both 157.3 and 157.5 fall within the GATE official accepted range. The rigorously calculated fundamental answer is 157.3 mm.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 157.3 mm | Accepted key range: 157.3 to 157.6

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q46
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question:
The speed-density relationship of a highway is given as

\[u = 100 - 0.5k\]

where, \(u\) = speed in km per hour, \(k\) = density in vehicles per km. The maximum flow (in vehicles per hour, round off to the nearest integer) is ______
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Flow Models

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Speed-density relationship: \(u = 100 - 0.5k\)
    • \(u\) = speed in km/h, \(k\) = density in vehicles/km
  • Aim: Calculate the maximum flow (\(q_{\text{max}}\)) in vehicles per hour.

3. Core Concepts:

Fundamental Traffic Equation:

\[q = u \cdot k \]

Greenshields Macroscopic Model: Assumes a linear relationship between speed and density.

\[u = u_f \left(1 - \dfrac{k}{k_j}\right) \]

Where \(u_f\) is free-flow speed and \(k_j\) is jam density.

Maximum Flow (\(q_{\text{max}}\)): Occurs at exactly half the free-flow speed and half the jam density (vertex of the flow-density parabola):

\[q_{\text{max}} = \dfrac{u_f \cdot k_j}{4} \]

4. Solution Method:

Method A (Direct Formula): Map the given equation to Greenshields format to extract \(u_f\) and \(k_j\), then use the \(q_{\text{max}}\) formula.

Method B (Calculus — First Principles): Express flow as a function of density, differentiate, and equate to zero.

5. Step-by-Step Execution (First Principles):

  1. Step 1: Setup flow equation\[q = u \cdot k = (100 - 0.5k) \cdot k = 100k - 0.5k^2 \]
  2. Step 2: Maximize flow
    Take the derivative of \(q\) with respect to \(k\) and set it to 0:\[\dfrac{dq}{dk} = 100 - k = 0 \implies k = 100\text{ veh/km} \](This is the optimum density \(k_0\) — exactly half the jam density \(k_j = 200\).)
  3. Step 3: Calculate maximum flow\[q_{\text{max}} = 100(100) - 0.5(100)^2 = 10000 - 5000 = 5000\text{ veh/h} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 5000 veh/h | Accepted key range: 5000 to 5000

options: penetration of bitumen at 25°C is between 20 and 40
viscosity of bitumen at 60°C is between 2400 and 3600 Poise
ductility of bitumen at 27°C is more than 30 cm
elastic recovery of bitumen at 15°C is more than 30%

structuredOptions.label: A
structuredOptions.text: penetration of bitumen at 25°C is between 20 and 40
structuredOptions.html: penetration of bitumen at 25°C is between 20 and 40

structuredOptions.label: B

structuredOptions.html: viscosity of bitumen at 60°C is between 2400 and 3600 Poise

structuredOptions.label: C
structuredOptions.text: ductility of bitumen at 27°C is more than 30 cm

structuredOptions.label: D

structuredOptions.html: elastic recovery of bitumen at 15°C is more than 30%

questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Highway Materials

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall
  • Given Data: Bitumen grade VG30 as per IS 73:2013.
  • Aim: Interpret the meaning of '30' in the VG30 designation.

3. Core Concepts:

Viscosity Grading (VG): In India, bitumen is graded by absolute viscosity at 60°C (IS 73:2013 — Paving Bitumen Specification). Grades: VG10, VG20, VG30, VG40. Viscosity is measured in Poise (P); \(1 \text{ P} = 0.1 \text{ Pa·s}\).

4. Solution Method:

Match the grade designation against the IS 73:2013 specification table.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

GradeViscosity at 60°C (Poise)
VG10800 – 1200
VG201600 – 2400
VG302400 – 3600
VG403200 – 4800
  • Option (A): Penetration — Incorrect. Penetration grading (e.g., 80/100) is the old system; VG is viscosity-based.
  • Option (B): Viscosity at 60°C between 2400 and 3600 Poise — Correct.
  • Option (C): Ductility — Incorrect. '30' does not refer to ductility.
  • Option (D): Elastic Recovery — Incorrect. This is a property of modified bitumen.

questions.question:
The speed-density relationship for a road section is shown in the figure.



The shape of the flow-density relationship is
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Engineering — Speed-Density Relationship

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: Linear speed-density (\(u\)-\(k\)) relationship (Greenshields model).
  • Aim: Determine the shape of the flow-density (\(q\)-\(k\)) curve.

3. Core Concepts:

Fundamental Equation of Traffic Flow: \(q = u \times k\)

Greenshields Linear Model:

\[u = u_f \left(1 - \dfrac{k}{k_j}\right) \]

where \(u_f\) = free flow speed, \(k_j\) = jam density.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Substitute the linear speed-density relation into \(q = uk\).
  2. Identify the mathematical form of the resulting equation.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Substitute\[q = u_f\!\left(1 - \dfrac{k}{k_j}\right) \times k \]
  2. Step 2: Expand\[q = u_f k - \dfrac{u_f}{k_j}k^2 \]\[q = -\left(\dfrac{u_f}{k_j}\right)k^2 + u_f k \]
  3. Step 3: Analyze Shape
    This is of the form \(q = -Ak^2 + Bk\) — a downward-opening parabola. The vertex corresponds to maximum flow (capacity) at optimum density \(k_{opt} = k_j/2\).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Parabolic | Correct option: (B)

Transportation Engineering | Traffic Engineering — Signalized Intersections

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Aim: Identify the defining characteristic of a well-designed signalized intersection.

3. Core Concepts:

Signal Design Objective: Manage conflicting traffic streams to ensure safety and minimize delay.

Cycle Time (\(C\)):

\[C = \sum (G_i + A_i + R_i) \]

where \(G_i\) = green time, \(A_i\) = amber/yellow time, \(R_i\) = all-red time for phase \(i\).

4. Solution Method:

Evaluate each option against traffic engineering principles.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  • Option (A): Crossing conflicts are increased — Incorrect. Signalization separates conflicting streams in time, reducing crossing conflicts.
  • Option (B): Total delay is minimized — Correct. A well-designed intersection optimizes cycle length and green split (e.g., Webster's method) to minimize overall user delay.

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 1 | CE Q34
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: A priority intersection has a single-lane one-way traffic road crossing an undivided two-lane two-way traffic road. The traffic stream speed on the single-lane road is 20 kmph and the speed on the two-lane road is 50 kmph. The perception-reaction time is 2.5 s, coefficient of longitudinal friction is 0.38 and acceleration due to gravity is 9.81 m/s². A clear sight triangle has to be ensured at this intersection. The minimum lengths of the sides of the sight triangle along the two-lane road and the single-lane road, respectively will be
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Sight Distance at Intersections

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Priority intersection (Uncontrolled/Yield/Stop behavior for minor road)
    • Major road: 2-lane, 2-way, \(v_{major} = 50 \text{ kmph}\)
    • Minor road: single-lane, 1-way, \(v_{minor} = 20 \text{ kmph}\)
    • Also given (red herrings): \(t_r = 2.5 \text{ s}\), \(f = 0.38\)
  • Aim: Minimum lengths of sight triangle sides along major and minor roads.

2. Core Concepts:

Common Pitfall: Many students will calculate the Stopping Sight Distance (SSD) for both roads using \(v t_r + v^2/2gf\), which yields ~61 m and 18 m (Option B). This formula is exclusively for uncontrolled intersections.

Code Reference (IRC:66-1976 — Sight Distance at Intersections): For a priority intersection (one road clearly designated as major), the crossing driver on the minor road must wait for a safe gap:

  • The minor road distance is fixed strictly at 15 meters (distance from the major road edge where the driver stops to observe).
  • The sight distance along the major road is the distance traveled by a vehicle at design speed over an 8-second time gap.

3. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Sight Triangle leg along the Minor Road
    Based on IRC:66 provision for priority intersections:\[d_{minor} = 15 \text{ m} \]
  2. Step 2: Sight Triangle leg along the Major Road
    Convert major road speed to m/s:\[v_{major} = 50 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = 13.889 \text{ m/s} \]Using the 8-second rule:\[d_{major} = 13.889 \times 8 = 111.11 \approx 111 \text{ m} \]

4. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 111 m and 15 m | Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 1 | CE Q54
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: Given the following data: design life \( n = 15 \) years, lane distribution factor \( D = 0.75 \), annual rate of growth of commercial vehicles \( r = 6\% \), vehicle damage factor \( F = 4 \) and initial traffic in the year of completion of construction = 3000 Commercial Vehicles Per Day (CVPD). As per IRC:37-2012, the design traffic in terms of cumulative number of standard axles (in million standard axles, up to two decimal places) is _______
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Pavement Design

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Design life: \(n = 15 \text{ years}\)
    • Lane distribution factor: \(D = 0.75\)
    • Annual growth rate: \(r = 6\% = 0.06\)
    • Vehicle damage factor: \(F = 4\)
    • Initial traffic in year of completion: \(A = 3000 \text{ CVPD}\)
  • Aim: Compute cumulative standard axles (\(N\)) in million standard axles (msa) per IRC:37-2012.

3. Core Concepts:

IRC:37-2012 Formula:

\[ N = \dfrac{365 \times A \times [(1+r)^n - 1]}{r} \times D \times F \]

where \(A\) = initial traffic (CVPD) in year of completion, \(r\) = annual growth rate (decimal), \(n\) = design life (years), \(D\) = lane distribution factor, \(F\) = vehicle damage factor.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate the compound growth multiplier \(\dfrac{(1+r)^n - 1}{r}\).
  2. Substitute all values into the IRC formula.
  3. Convert the result to million standard axles (msa).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Growth Multiplier\[(1.06)^{15} = 2.396558 \]\[\text{Multiplier} = \dfrac{2.396558 - 1}{0.06} = \dfrac{1.396558}{0.06} = 23.276 \]
  2. Step 2: Apply IRC Formula\[N = 365 \times 3000 \times 23.276 \times 0.75 \times 4 \]\[N = 1{,}095{,}000 \times 23.276 \times 3 = 76{,}461{,}561 \text{ standard axles} \]
  3. Step 3: Convert to msa\[N_{msa} = \dfrac{76{,}461{,}561}{10^6} \approx 76.46 \text{ msa} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 76.46 msa | Accepted key range: 75.00 to 78.00

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 1 | CE Q55
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: An aircraft approaches the threshold of a runway strip at a speed of 200 km/h. The pilot decelerates the aircraft at a rate of 1.697 m/s² and takes 18 s to exit the runway strip. If the deceleration after exiting the runway is 1 m/s², then the distance (in m, up to one decimal place) of the gate position from the location of exit on the runway is _______
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Airport Engineering

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Approach speed: \(V_1 = 200 \text{ km/h}\)
    • Deceleration on runway: \(a_1 = -1.697 \text{ m/s}^2\)
    • Time on runway before exit: \(t_1 = 18 \text{ s}\)
    • Deceleration on taxiway: \(a_2 = -1 \text{ m/s}^2\)
    • Final speed at gate: \(V_3 = 0 \text{ m/s}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the distance from runway exit to the gate (\(D_2\)) in meters.

3. Core Concepts:

This is a sequential 1D linear kinematics problem.

  • Velocity-Time: \(v = u + at\) — to find speed at exit
  • Velocity-Displacement: \(v^2 - u^2 = 2as\) — to find stopping distance on taxiway
  • Unit conversion: \(1 \text{ km/h} = \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m/s}\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Convert \(V_1\) from km/h to m/s.
  2. Calculate exit speed \(V_2\) using runway kinematics.
  3. Use \(V_2\) as initial speed for taxiway phase; solve for \(D_2\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Convert Approach Speed\[V_1 = 200 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = 55.556 \text{ m/s} \]
  2. Step 2: Speed at Runway Exit (\(V_2\))\[V_2 = V_1 + a_1 t_1 = 55.556 + (-1.697 \times 18) = 55.556 - 30.546 = 25.010 \text{ m/s} \]
  3. Step 3: Taxiway Distance (\(D_2\))\[V_3^2 - V_2^2 = 2a_2 D_2 \]\[0 - (25.010)^2 = 2(-1)D_2 \]\[D_2 = \dfrac{625.48}{2} = 312.74 \text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 312.7 m | Accepted key range: 311.0 to 319.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q16

questions.question: Peak Hour Factor (PHF) is used to represent the proportion of peak sub-hourly traffic flow within the peak hour. If 15-minute sub-hours are considered, the theoretically possible range of PHF will be
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Engineering — Peak Hour Factor

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Peak Hour Factor (PHF) based on 15-minute sub-hour intervals (4 intervals per hour).
  • Aim: Determine the theoretically possible numerical range of PHF.

3. Core Concepts:

Peak Hour Factor (PHF) — Highway Capacity Manual (HCM):\[PHF = \dfrac{V}{4 \times V_{15}}\]where \(V\) = total peak hour volume (veh/hr); \(V_{15}\) = maximum 15-minute volume within that hour; 4 = number of 15-minute intervals per hour.

4. Solution Method:

Find the bounds by evaluating two extreme traffic scenarios: (1) perfectly uniform flow, and (2) all vehicles concentrated in a single 15-minute interval.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Upper Limit (Uniform Flow):
    If \(v_1 = v_2 = v_3 = v_4 = V_{15}\), then \(V = 4 \times V_{15}\):\[PHF = \dfrac{4 \times V_{15}}{4 \times V_{15}} = 1.0\]
  2. Lower Limit (Concentrated Flow):
    If \(v_1 = V_{15}\) and \(v_2 = v_3 = v_4 = 0\), then \(V = V_{15}\):\[PHF = \dfrac{V_{15}}{4 \times V_{15}} = \dfrac{1}{4} = 0.25\]
  3. Theoretical range: \(0.25 \le PHF \le 1.0\)

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.25 to 1.0 | Correct option: (C)

questions.question: As per IRC:37-2012, in order to control subgrade rutting in flexible pavements, the parameter to be considered is

vertical compressive strain on top of subgrade
vertical compressive stress on top of granular layer
vertical deflection at the surface of the pavement

structuredOptions.label: B
structuredOptions.text: vertical compressive strain on top of subgrade
structuredOptions.html: vertical compressive strain on top of subgrade

structuredOptions.label: C

structuredOptions.html: vertical compressive stress on top of granular layer

structuredOptions.label: D
structuredOptions.text: vertical deflection at the surface of the pavement
structuredOptions.html: vertical deflection at the surface of the pavement

questions.explanation:
Pavement Engineering | Flexible Pavement Design Criteria per IRC:37-2012

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall
  • Given Data: IRC:37-2012 guidelines for flexible pavement design; objective: control subgrade rutting.
  • Aim: Identify the critical parameter for controlling subgrade rutting.

3. Core Concepts:

IRC:37-2012 employs a mechanistic-empirical approach with two primary failure criteria:

Failure ModeCritical LocationControlling Parameter
Fatigue CrackingBottom of bituminous layerHorizontal tensile strain (\(\varepsilon_t\))
Subgrade RuttingTop of subgradeVertical compressive strain (\(\varepsilon_v\))

Key Provision (IRC:37-2012, Clause 8.2):\[\varepsilon_v \leq \varepsilon_{v,allowable} = 1.0 \times 10^{-4} \times \left(\dfrac{1}{N}\right)^{0.22}\]where \(N\) = cumulative standard axles.

  2. IRC:37-2012 explicitly states that vertical compressive strain at the top of subgrade is the critical parameter to limit rutting.

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q35
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: A car follows a slow moving truck (travelling at a speed of 10 m/s) on a two-lane two-way highway. The car reduces its speed to 10 m/s and follows the truck maintaining a distance of 16 m from the truck. On finding a clear gap in the opposing traffic stream, the car accelerates at an average rate of 4 m/s², overtakes the truck and returns to its original lane. When it returns to its original lane, the distance between the car and the truck is 16 m. The total distance covered by the car during this period (from the time it leaves its lane and subsequently returns to its lane after overtaking) is
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Highway Geometric Design

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Speed of truck: \(v_t = 10\text{ m/s}\) (Constant)
    • Initial speed of car: \(v_c = 10\text{ m/s}\)
    • Acceleration of car during overtaking: \(a = 4\text{ m/s}^2\)
    • Initial gap maintained before overtaking: \(s_1 = 16\text{ m}\)
    • Final gap maintained after returning to lane: \(s_2 = 16\text{ m}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the total distance covered by the car from leaving its lane to returning after overtaking.

3. Core Concepts:

Relative Kinematics: To safely overtake, the car must cover the relative distance of both initial and final gaps with respect to the moving truck.
(Note: Per standard IRC Overtaking Sight Distance analysis, since specific vehicle lengths aren't provided, the relative distance to clear is simply the sum of the gaps.)

Equations of Motion:\[S_{rel} = u_{rel}\,t + \dfrac{1}{2}a_{rel}\,t^2\]\[S_{car} = v_c\,t + \dfrac{1}{2}a_{car}\,t^2\]

4. Solution Method:

Calculate the overtaking maneuver time (\(t\)) by analyzing the relative motion between the car and the truck. Once \(t\) is obtained, compute the absolute distance covered by the car using its own acceleration and initial velocity.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Define Relative Variables:
    • Relative initial velocity: \(u_{rel} = 10 - 10 = 0\text{ m/s}\)
    • Relative acceleration: \(a_{rel} = 4 - 0 = 4\text{ m/s}^2\)
    • Total relative distance to be covered: \(S_{rel} = s_1 + s_2 = 16 + 16 = 32\text{ m}\)
  2. Calculate Time to Overtake (\(t\)):\[S_{rel} = u_{rel}\,t + \dfrac{1}{2}a_{rel}\,t^2\]\[32 = 0 \cdot t + \dfrac{1}{2}(4)t^2\]\[32 = 2t^2 \implies t^2 = 16 \implies t = 4\text{ seconds}\]
  3. Calculate Total Absolute Distance Covered by the Car (\(S_{car}\)):\[S_{car} = v_c\,t + \dfrac{1}{2}a\,t^2\]\[S_{car} = (10 \times 4) + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times (4)^2\]\[S_{car} = 40 + 2(16) = 40 + 32 = 72\text{ m}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 72 m | Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q53
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: The space mean speed (kmph) and density (vehicles/km) of a traffic stream are linearly related. The free flow speed and jam density are 80 kmph and 100 vehicles/km respectively. The traffic flow (in vehicles/h, up to one decimal place) corresponding to a speed of 40 kmph is ______
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Engineering

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Linear relation between speed and density (Greenshields Model)
    • Free flow speed: \(v_f = 80\text{ kmph}\)
    • Jam density: \(k_j = 100\text{ vehicles/km}\)
    • Operating speed: \(v = 40\text{ kmph}\)
  • Aim: Find the traffic flow (\(q\)) in vehicles/h corresponding to a speed of 40 kmph.

3. Core Concepts:

Greenshields Macroscopic Stream Model: Assumes a linear relationship between space mean speed (\(v\)) and density (\(k\)).\[v = v_f \left(1 - \dfrac{k}{k_j}\right)\]

Fundamental Traffic Equation:\[q = k \times v\]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Substitute given \(v_f\) and \(k_j\) into the Greenshields model.
  2. Use target speed (\(v = 40\text{ kmph}\)) to solve for density (\(k\)).
  3. Multiply calculated \(k\) by \(v\) to find flow (\(q\)).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Determine Density (\(k\)) at \(v = 40\text{ kmph}\):\[40 = 80\left(1 - \dfrac{k}{100}\right)\]\[0.5 = 1 - \dfrac{k}{100} \implies k = 50\text{ vehicles/km}\]
  2. Determine Traffic Flow (\(q\)):\[q = k \times v = 50\text{ veh/km} \times 40\text{ km/h} = 2000\text{ vehicles/h}\]Note: The speed 40 kmph is exactly half of \(v_f = 80\text{ kmph}\), corresponding to the maximum capacity:\[q_{max} = \dfrac{v_f \times k_j}{4} = \dfrac{80 \times 100}{4} = 2000\text{ veh/h}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2000.0 veh/h | Accepted key range: 2000.0 to 2000.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q54
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: A 7.5 m wide two-lane road on a plain terrain is to be laid along a horizontal curve of radius 510 m. For a design speed of 100 kmph, super-elevation is provided as per IRC: 73-1980. Consider acceleration due to gravity as 9.81 m/s². The level difference between the inner and outer edges of the road (in m, up to three decimal places) is ______
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Highway Engineering

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Road width: \(W = 7.5\text{ m}\) (Two-lane)
    • Terrain: Plain
    • Horizontal curve radius: \(R = 510\text{ m}\)
    • Design speed: \(V = 100\text{ kmph}\)
    • \(g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2\)
    • Design Code: IRC 73-1980
  • Aim: Calculate the level difference between the inner and outer edges of the fully super-elevated road.

3. Core Concepts:

Super-elevation Design as per IRC:

  1. Calculate theoretical super-elevation (\(e_{calc}\)) for 75% of design speed, completely neglecting lateral friction:\[e_{calc} = \dfrac{(0.75 \times v)^2}{g \times R}\]
  2. Check against maximum allowable limit. For plain and rolling terrain: \(e_{max} = 0.07\) (7%).
  3. If \(e_{calc} > 0.07\), limit provision to \(0.07\) and check if required lateral friction \(f \le 0.15\).

Level Difference (\(E\)): \(E = e_{provided} \times W\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Convert design speed from kmph to m/s.
  2. Compute \(e_{calc}\) using the fundamental formula.
  3. Compare \(e_{calc}\) with IRC limit (0.07) to find the provided \(e\).
  4. Check lateral friction (\(f\)) at full design speed to ensure safety.
  5. Multiply the provided \(e\) by the pavement width to get the level difference.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Velocity Conversion:\[v = 100 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = 27.778\text{ m/s}\]
  2. Theoretical Super-elevation (\(e_{calc}\)):\[e_{calc} = \dfrac{(0.75 \times 27.778)^2}{9.81 \times 510} = \dfrac{(20.8335)^2}{5003.1} = \dfrac{434.03}{5003.1} = 0.08675\]Since \(e_{calc}\,(0.08675) > e_{max}\,(0.07)\) for plain terrain, restrict to \(e_{provided} = 0.07\).
  3. Check Lateral Friction (\(f\)):\[e_{provided} + f_{req} = \dfrac{v^2}{gR} = \dfrac{(27.778)^2}{9.81 \times 510} = \dfrac{771.61}{5003.1} = 0.1542\]\[f_{req} = 0.1542 - 0.07 = 0.0842\]Since \(f_{req}\,(0.0842) < f_{max}\,(0.15)\), providing \(e = 0.07\) is safe and no speed restriction is needed.
  4. Level Difference (\(E\)):\[E = e_{provided} \times W = 0.07 \times 7.5\text{ m} = 0.525\text{ m}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.525 m | Accepted key range: 0.520 to 0.530

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q16
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: A super-elevation \(e\) is provided on a circular horizontal curve such that a vehicle can be stopped on the curve without sliding. Assuming a design speed \(v\) and maximum coefficient of side friction \(f_{max}\), which one of the following criteria should be satisfied?
options: no limit on \(e\) can be set

structuredOptions.label: C
structuredOptions.text: no limit on \(e\) can be set
structuredOptions.html: no limit on \(e\) can be set

questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Highway Geometric Design

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: Super-elevation \(= e\); vehicle stopped on curve (\(v = 0\)); maximum coefficient of side friction \(= f_{max}\).
  • Aim: Determine the criterion to prevent the stationary vehicle from sliding inward.

3. Core Concepts:

General equilibrium on a super-elevated curve: \(e + f = v^2/(gR)\).

When \(v = 0\): no centrifugal force. The vehicle tends to slide inward (down the transverse slope) due to gravity.

  • Force pulling vehicle inward: \(W\sin\theta \approx W \cdot e\) (small angles)
  • Max friction resisting slide: \(f_{max} \cdot W\cos\theta \approx f_{max} \cdot W\)

Condition for no sliding: \(W \cdot e \le f_{max} \cdot W \implies e \le f_{max}\)

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Substitute \(v = 0\): centrifugal force \(P = 0\).
  2. Net force along pavement (downward slope) \(= W\sin\theta\).
  3. Max friction \(= f_{max} W\cos\theta\).
  4. No-sliding condition: \(\tan\theta \le f_{max}\).
  5. Since \(e = \tan\theta\): \(\boxed{e \le f_{max}}\)

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(e \le f_{max}\)  |  Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q17
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: A runway is being constructed in a new airport as per the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) recommendations. The elevation and the airport reference temperature of this airport are 535 m above the mean sea level and 22.65°C, respectively. Consider the effective gradient of runway as 1%. The length of runway required for a design-aircraft under the standard conditions is 2000 m. Within the framework of applying sequential corrections as per the ICAO recommendations, the length of runway corrected for the temperature is
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Airport Engineering

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Elevation above MSL: \(h = 535\text{ m}\)
    • Airport Reference Temperature (ART): \(22.65^\circ\text{C}\)
    • Basic runway length: \(L_0 = 2000\text{ m}\)
  • Aim: Calculate runway length corrected sequentially for elevation and temperature (per ICAO).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Elevation Correction: Increase basic length by \(7\%\) per \(300\text{ m}\) rise above MSL.
    \[L_1 = L_0\left(1 + 0.07 \times \dfrac{h}{300}\right) \]
  • Temperature Correction: Increase \(L_1\) by \(1\%\) per \(1^\circ\text{C}\) above Standard Airport Temperature (SAT).
    \[SAT_{airport} = 15 - 0.0065 \times h \]\[L_2 = L_1\left(1 + 0.01 \times \Delta T\right) \]

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Elevation correction:
    \[\text{Correction}_1 = 2000 \times 0.07 \times \dfrac{535}{300} = 249.67\text{ m} \]\[L_1 = 2000 + 249.67 = 2249.67\text{ m} \]
  2. SAT at airport elevation:
    \[SAT = 15 - (0.0065 \times 535) = 15 - 3.4775 = 11.52^\circ\text{C} \]
  3. Temperature difference:

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Cycle length: \(C = 96\text{ s}\)
    • Effective green time: \(g = 36\text{ s}\)
    • From Queue length vs. time graph:
      • Red phase ends at \(t = 60\text{ s}\) \(\implies\) effective red time \(r = 60\text{ s}\)
      • Maximum queue length at \(t = 60\text{ s}\): \(Q_{max} = 10\text{ vehicles}\)
      • Queue clears completely at \(t = 90\text{ s}\)
  • Aim: Determine the uniform arrival rate (\(v\)), saturation flow rate (\(s\)), and the average stopped delay per vehicle for this cycle.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Arrival & Departure Mechanics: During effective red time (\(r\)), vehicles arrive at rate \(v\) and form a queue. During effective green time (\(g\)), vehicles arrive at rate \(v\) and depart at saturation flow rate \(s\). Net discharge rate is \((s - v)\).
  • Queue Length Formulas:
    • Max queue length: \(Q_{max} = v \times r\)
    • Queue clearance: \(Q_{max} = (s - v) \times t_c\), where \(t_c\) is the time to clear the queue after green starts.
  • Delay Calculation: Total stopped delay = area under the Queue-Time curve.
    \[\text{Average Delay} = \dfrac{\text{Total Delay}}{\text{Total Vehicles Arriving in One Cycle}} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Use red time and max queue length from the graph to find arrival rate (\(v\)).
  2. Use queue clearance time (\(t = 60\) to \(t = 90\)) to find the saturation flow rate (\(s\)).
  3. Calculate the area of the triangle to find total delay.
  4. Calculate total vehicles arriving in the 96 s cycle.
  5. Divide total delay by total vehicles to get average stopped delay.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Determine uniform arrival rate (\(v\)):
    During \(t = 0\) to \(t = 60\text{ s}\), light is red.
    \[Q_{max} = v \times 60 = 10 \implies v = \dfrac{10}{60}\text{ veh/s} = 600\text{ vph} \]
  2. Determine saturation flow rate (\(s\)):
    Clearance time \(t_c = 90 - 60 = 30\text{ s}\).
    \[(s - v) \times 30 = 10 \implies 30s - 5 = 10 \implies s = \dfrac{15}{30} = 0.5\text{ veh/s} \]\[s = 0.5 \times 3600 = 1800\text{ vph} \]
  3. Calculate average stopped delay:
    Total delay = area of triangle under the queue-time graph:
    \[\text{Total delay} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 90\text{ s} \times 10\text{ veh} = 450\text{ veh-sec} \]Total vehicles arriving per cycle:
    \[N = v \times C = \dfrac{10}{60} \times 96 = 16\text{ vehicles} \]Average delay:
    \[\text{Average delay} = \dfrac{450}{16} = 28.125\text{ s/vehicle} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(s = 1800\text{ vph}\), average stopped delay per vehicle \(= 28.125\text{ s}\)  |  Correct option: (B)

questions.question: The radius of a horizontal circular curve on a highway is 120 m. The design speed is 60 km/hour, and the design coefficient of lateral friction between the tyre and the road surface is 0.15. The estimated value of superelevation required (if full lateral friction is assumed to develop), and the value of coefficient of friction needed (if no superelevation is provided) will, respectively, be
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Highway Engineering - Horizontal Alignment

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Radius of horizontal curve: \(R = 120\text{ m}\)
    • Design speed: \(V = 60\text{ km/h}\)
    • Design coefficient of lateral friction: \(f = 0.15\)
  • Aim: Find the required superelevation (\(e_{req}\)) if full friction is developed, and the required friction (\(f_{req}\)) if no superelevation is provided.

3. Core Concepts:

  • General Equation for Horizontal Curve:
    \[e + f = \dfrac{V^2}{127R} \]where \(e\) = rate of superelevation, \(f\) = coefficient of lateral friction, \(V\) = speed in km/h, \(R\) = radius in meters, and \(\dfrac{V^2}{127R}\) represents the total centrifugal ratio (Impact Factor).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Compute the total centrifugal ratio \(\dfrac{V^2}{127R}\).
  2. For \(e_{req}\), subtract the full available friction (\(f = 0.15\)) from the centrifugal ratio.
  3. For \(f_{req}\), assume \(e = 0\) and equate friction directly to the centrifugal ratio.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate total centrifugal ratio:
    \[\dfrac{V^2}{127R} = \dfrac{60^2}{127 \times 120} = \dfrac{3600}{15240} \approx 0.23622 \]
  2. Calculate superelevation required (\(e_{req}\)) — full friction developed:
    \[e_{req} + 0.15 = 0.23622 \implies e_{req} = 0.08622 \]Represented as \(\dfrac{1}{n}\): \(\dfrac{1}{0.08622} \approx 11.6 \implies e_{req} = \dfrac{1}{11.6}\)
  3. Calculate friction required (\(f_{req}\)) — no superelevation:
    \[0 + f_{req} = 0.23622 \implies f_{req} \approx 0.24 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(e_{req} = \dfrac{1}{11.6}\) and \(f_{req} = 0.24\)  |  Correct option: (C)

questions.question: While aligning a hill road with a ruling gradient of 6%, a horizontal curve of radius 50 m is encountered. The grade compensation (in percentage, up to two decimal places) to be provided for this case would be ___________

IRC Code Provisions (IRC: 73):

  • Theoretical grade compensation: \(GC = \dfrac{30 + R}{R}\%\)
  • Maximum allowable limit: \(GC_{\text{max}} = \dfrac{75}{R}\%\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Compute the formula-based GC.
  2. Compute the maximum allowable GC.
  3. Adopt the minimum of the two as the final grade compensation.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Formula-based GC:\[GC = \dfrac{30 + 50}{50} = \dfrac{80}{50} = 1.60\% \]
  2. Maximum allowable GC:\[GC_{\text{max}} = \dfrac{75}{50} = 1.50\% \]

Final Answer: 1.50% | Accepted key range: 1.49 to 1.51

questions.question:
Two cars P and Q are moving in a racing track continuously for two hours. Assume that no other vehicles are using the track during this time. The expressions relating the distance travelled d (in km) and time t (in hour) for both the vehicles are given as
P: \( d = 60t \)
Q: \( d = 60t^2 \)
Within the first one hour, the maximum space headway would be
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Engineering

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Distance equations: \(d_P = 60t\) and \(d_Q = 60t^2\) (where \(d\) is in km, \(t\) is in hours)
    • Time domain: First one hour (\(t \in [0, 1]\))
  • Aim: Find the maximum space headway between cars P and Q within the first hour.

3. Core Concepts:

Space Headway (\(S\)): The physical distance between two vehicles at any given time \(t\):\[S(t) = |d_P(t) - d_Q(t)| \]

Calculus for Optimization: To find the maximum value of a continuous function on a closed interval, set its first derivative to zero (\(dS/dt = 0\)) to find critical points, and check the boundaries.

4. Solution Method:

  • For \(t \in [0, 1]\), \(t \ge t^2\), meaning car P is strictly ahead of or level with car Q (\(60t \ge 60t^2\)).
  • Formulate the headway function: \(S(t) = 60t - 60t^2\).
  • Differentiate \(S(t)\) with respect to \(t\) and equate to zero to find the time of maximum separation.
  • Substitute this time back into \(S(t)\) to find the maximum distance.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Formulate Equation: \(S(t) = 60t - 60t^2\)
  2. First Derivative: \(\dfrac{dS}{dt} = 60 - 120t\)
  3. Find Critical Time:\[60 - 120t = 0 \implies t = 0.5 \text{ hours} = 30 \text{ minutes} \]
  4. Check Second Derivative (Sanity Check):
    \(\dfrac{d^2S}{dt^2} = -120\) — since it is negative, this confirms a local maximum.
  5. Calculate Maximum Headway:\[S(0.5) = 60(0.5) - 60(0.5)^2 = 30 - 60(0.25) = 30 - 15 = 15 \text{ km} \]Maximum headway is 15 km occurring at 30 minutes.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 15 km at 30 minutes | Correct option: (A)

  1. Mechanical Widening (same for both speeds):\[W_{me} = \dfrac{2 \times 5^2}{2 \times 50} = \dfrac{50}{100} = 0.50\text{ m} \]
  2. Psychological Widening at 60 kmph:\[W_{ps,60} = \dfrac{60}{9.5\sqrt{50}} = \dfrac{60}{9.5 \times 7.071} = \dfrac{60}{67.175} = 0.893\text{ m} \]
  3. Psychological Widening at 80 kmph:\[W_{ps,80} = \dfrac{80}{9.5\sqrt{50}} = \dfrac{80}{67.175} = 1.191\text{ m} \]
  4. Summary:
    Speed\(W_{me}\) (m)\(W_{ps}\) (m)
    60 kmph0.500.893
    80 kmph0.501.191

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(w_{me,60} = 0.50\text{ m},\; w_{ps,60} = 0.89\text{ m},\; w_{me,80} = 0.50\text{ m},\; w_{ps,80} = 1.19\text{ m}\) | Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2016 Set 1 | CE Q54
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: While traveling along and against the traffic stream, a moving observer measured the relative flows as 50 vehicles/hr and 200 vehicles/hr, respectively. The average speeds of the moving observer while traveling along and against the stream are 20 km/hr and 30 km/hr, respectively. The density of the traffic stream (expressed in vehicles/km) is _______________
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Engineering — Moving Observer Method

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Against stream: observer speed \(v_a = 30\text{ km/hr}\), relative flow \(Q_a = 200\text{ veh/hr}\)
    • With stream: observer speed \(v_w = 20\text{ km/hr}\), relative flow \(Q_w = 50\text{ veh/hr}\)
  • Aim: Calculate traffic stream density (\(k\)) in veh/km.

3. Core Concepts:

Moving Observer Method equations relating flow (\(q\)), density (\(k\)), observer speed (\(v_{obs}\)), and relative flow (\(Q\)):

  • Against traffic: \(Q_a = q + k\,v_a\)
  • With traffic (stream faster than observer): \(Q_w = q - k\,v_w\)

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. System of equations:\[q + 30k = 200 \quad \cdots (1) \]\[q - 20k = 50 \quad \cdots (2) \]
  2. Subtract (2) from (1) to eliminate \(q\):\[50k = 150 \implies k = 3\text{ veh/km} \]
  3. Sanity Check:
    From (1): \(q = 200 - 30(3) = 110\text{ veh/hr}\)
    Stream speed: \(v = q/k = 110/3 = 36.67\text{ km/hr} > 20\text{ km/hr}\) ✓ (validates assumption for Eq. 2)

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 3.0 veh/km | Accepted key range: [2.9, 3.1]

questions.title: GATE CE 2016 Set 2 | CE Q21
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question:
In the context of the IRC 58-2011 guidelines for rigid pavement design, consider the following pair of statements.

I: Radius of relative stiffness is directly related to modulus of elasticity of concrete and inversely related to Poisson's ratio
II: Radius of relative stiffness is directly related to thickness of slab and modulus of subgrade reaction.

Which one of the following combinations is correct?
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Rigid Pavement Design

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Aim: Evaluate the truth of two statements about Westergaard's Radius of relative stiffness (\(l\)).

3. Core Concepts:

According to Westergaard's theory (IRC 58), the Radius of relative stiffness (\(l\)) is:

\[ l = \left[\dfrac{Eh^3}{12k(1-\mu^2)}\right]^{1/4} \]
  • \(E\) = Modulus of elasticity of concrete
  • \(h\) = Thickness of concrete slab
  • \(k\) = Modulus of subgrade reaction
  • \(\mu\) = Poisson's ratio of concrete

4. Solution Method & Execution:

  • Statement I: As \(\mu\) increases, \((1-\mu^2)\) decreases, making the fraction larger, thus increasing \(l\). So \(l\) is directly (not inversely) related to \(\mu\). → Statement I is False.
  • Statement II: \(l \propto k^{-1/4}\), meaning higher \(k\) gives lower \(l\) (inversely related). The statement claims direct relation to \(k\). → Statement II is False.

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Statement I: False; Statement II: False | Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2016 Set 2 | CE Q53
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: The critical flow ratios for a three-phase signal are found to be 0.30, 0.25, and 0.25. The total time lost in the cycle is 10 s. Pedestrian crossings at this junction are not significant. The respective Green times (expressed in seconds and rounded off to the nearest integer) for the three phases are
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Engineering

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Critical flow ratios: \(y_1 = 0.30\), \(y_2 = 0.25\), \(y_3 = 0.25\)
    • Total lost time per cycle: \(L = 10\text{ s}\)
    • Pedestrian clearance is insignificant.
  • Aim: Find the effective Green times (\(g_1, g_2, g_3\)) in seconds, rounded to the nearest integer.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Webster's Method for Signal Design: Optimum Cycle Length:\[C_0 = \dfrac{1.5L + 5}{1 - Y} \]where \(Y = \sum y_i\) is the sum of critical flow ratios.
  • Effective Green Time Split: Total effective green time \(T_e = C_0 - L\), allocated proportionally:\[g_i = \dfrac{y_i}{Y} \times T_e \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Determine \(Y\) (sum of flow ratios).
  2. Calculate optimum cycle length \(C_0\).
  3. Find total effective green time (\(T_e\)).
  4. Proportionally distribute \(T_e\) for each phase.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Sum of Flow Ratios (\(Y\)):\[Y = 0.30 + 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.80 \]
  2. Optimum Cycle Length (\(C_0\)):\[C_0 = \dfrac{1.5 \times 10 + 5}{1 - 0.80} = \dfrac{20}{0.20} = 100\text{ s} \]
  3. Total Effective Green Time (\(T_e\)):\[T_e = 100 - 10 = 90\text{ s} \]
  4. Phase Green Times:\[g_1 = \dfrac{0.30}{0.80} \times 90 = 33.75 \approx 34\text{ s} \]\[g_2 = \dfrac{0.25}{0.80} \times 90 = 28.125 \approx 28\text{ s} \]\[g_3 = \dfrac{0.25}{0.80} \times 90 = 28.125 \approx 28\text{ s} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(g_1 = 34\text{ s}\), \(g_2 = 28\text{ s}\), \(g_3 = 28\text{ s}\) | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2016 Set 2 | CE Q54
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: A motorist traveling at 100 km/h on a highway needs to take the next exit, which has a speed limit of 50 km/h. The section of the roadway before the ramp entry has a downgrade of 3% and coefficient of friction (f) is 0.35. In order to enter the ramp at the maximum allowable speed limit, the braking distance (expressed in m) from the exit ramp is _________
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Highway Engineering

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Initial speed: \(v_1 = 100\text{ km/h}\)
    • Final speed on ramp: \(v_2 = 50\text{ km/h}\)
    • Gradient: Downgrade of \(3\%\) → \(n = 0.03\)
    • Coefficient of longitudinal friction: \(f = 0.35\)
    • \(g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2\)
  • Aim: Determine the necessary braking distance in meters.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Work-Energy Principle for Braking: The kinetic energy change is equated to the work done by friction and gravity.
  • Formula:\[S = \dfrac{v_1^2 - v_2^2}{2g(f \pm n)} \]Since it is a downgrade, gravity works against braking, so we use the minus sign (\(-\)).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Convert speeds from km/h to m/s.
  2. Formulate the braking distance using the adjusted deceleration coefficient \((f - n)\).
  3. Execute the calculation.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Velocity Conversions:\[v_1 = 100 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = 27.778\text{ m/s} \]\[v_2 = 50 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = 13.889\text{ m/s} \]
  2. Apply Braking Distance Equation:\[S = \dfrac{v_1^2 - v_2^2}{2g(f - n)} = \dfrac{(27.778)^2 - (13.889)^2}{2 \times 9.81 \times (0.35 - 0.03)} \]
  3. Compute:\[\text{Numerator} = 771.605 - 192.904 = 578.701\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2 \]\[\text{Denominator} = 19.62 \times 0.32 = 6.2784\text{ m/s}^2 \]\[S = \dfrac{578.701}{6.2784} = 92.17\text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 92.17 m | Accepted key range: 92 to 93

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 1 | CE Q32

questions.question: The penetration value of a bitumen sample tested at 25°C is 80. When this sample is heated to 60°C and tested again, the needle of the penetration test apparatus penetrates the bitumen sample by \(d\) mm. The value of \(d\) CANNOT be less than __________ mm.

    • Sample re-tested at \(60^\circ\text{C}\), yielding depth \(d\text{ mm}\)
  • Aim: Determine the physical lower boundary threshold for depth \(d\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Bitumen Penetration Test (IS 1203): Measures depth of penetration of a standardized needle (100 g, 5 s). The penetration value is expressed in tenths of a millimeter (0.1 mm).
  • Temperature Susceptibility: Bitumen is thermoplastic — viscosity decreases as temperature increases, leading to greater needle penetration (softer state).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Convert the penetration value at \(25^\circ\text{C}\) to absolute depth in mm.
  2. Conclude that the higher temperature forces greater penetration, so \(d\) must exceed the baseline depth.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Convert value to depth:

  2. Compare conditions:
    Since \(60^\circ\text{C} \gg 25^\circ\text{C}\), the bitumen is softer at \(60^\circ\text{C}\), providing less resistance to the needle.
    \[d > 8\text{ mm} \]

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data: Four potential descriptive conditions of free flow speed (\(u_f\)).
  • Aim: Identify the logically FALSE statement.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Free Flow Speed (\(u_f\)): Theoretical upper speed limit when traffic is completely unhindered (\(q \to 0\), \(k \to 0\)). Depends only on road geometry and pavement friction.
  • Critical/Optimum Speed (\(u_c\)): The speed at which maximum flow (capacity) occurs. In the linear Greenshields model, \(u_c = u_f/2\), which is strictly less than \(u_f\).
